stories.headline: Colorado's 2026 elections defy history as Democrats hold wide advantages, analysts say
stories.summary:
Political scientists Ken Cronin and Tom Loevy write that Colorado, once reliably Republican in presidential contests, has become a solidly Democratic state. Presidents Eisenhower, Nixon, Reagan and George W. Bush all carried it, but Democrats have won in recent presidential elections.

Two U.S. House races are considered competitive in the Nov. 3 election. District 8, running from north of Denver to Greeley, was designed to be evenly split between Republican and Democratic voters. District 5, centered on El Paso County and Colorado Springs, is historically Republican but is hosting a competitive race, even though Republicans hold about 55,000 more registered voters there. Both races are expected to be decided by unaffiliated voters.

The authors predict Democrat Manny Rutinel will defeat Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in District 8, and Republican Rep. Jeff Crank will defeat Democrat Jessica Killin in District 5. They also expect Democrat Phil Weiser to win the governor's race and Sen. John Hickenlooper to win reelection, calling the Democratic advantage unprecedented in modern Colorado history.

stories.headline: Medical groups and fundraising stack up against Proposition 135 ban on gender-affirming surgeries for minors
stories.summary:
Colorado voters will decide in the coming weeks whether to ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors under Proposition 135. Available data suggests few teens receive such procedures in the state, and no Colorado hospitals currently offer them to minors.

Medical provider groups oppose the measure, citing concerns about government interference in health care decisions. Opponents also held a significant fundraising advantage as of the end of September. Patricia McKernan, director of the Protect Kids Colorado committee, which helped place the question on the ballot, said children lack the maturity to make decisions affecting future fertility.

Thornton resident Chris Cook, whose transgender daughter may need extended-release puberty-blocking implants, said he fears the measure's vague language could restrict that care. Nationally, 26 states outlaw both gender-affirming medication and surgery for youth, and the Trump administration has pushed to halt such care for minors, with at least six hospitals agreeing to stop providing it.

stories.headline: How gang violence in Denver's Guyton family furthers the crime cycle
stories.summary:
A Denver Post investigation traces the Guyton family's history of gang violence over four decades. Urocca Guyton, a Denver gang member who fathered nearly two dozen children, was first charged with a crime at 13. Jurors acquitted him of a 2015 murder, and he was shot and killed in 2018 outside a Leetsdale Drive nightclub at age 31.

Three of his teenage sons have since been charged with murder in separate killings. Remi Cordova killed Pamela Cabriales on Colfax Avenue in 2021 at age 14. Johntae Guyton killed Ramon Castro Contreras in Lakewood in 2022 at 17. A third son, charged as a juvenile and not named, is accused of killing 13-year-old Ja'Loynie Cosey in 2025.

The Post reviewed nearly 900 pages of records and interviewed nearly two dozen people, finding themes of gang violence, addiction and systemic failures. Some relatives have recovered and are working to break the cycle of generational pain.

stories.headline: Denver man sentenced to 30 months in federal prison for COVID relief scheme
stories.summary:
Steve Randall Howe, 74, of Denver was sentenced Oct. 14 to two and a half years in federal prison for fraudulently obtaining more than $1.2 million in pandemic relief funds. He pleaded guilty about five months earlier to one count of bank fraud and one count of money laundering.

According to the U.S. Attorney's Office, Howe obtained $1,243,799.91 in Paycheck Protection Program loans from six banks between April 2020 and January 2022. He lied about employee counts and payroll at his businesses, most of which had no function or employees, and submitted sham tax and payroll records.

He spent the money on a new home, retail purchases, travel, transfers to China, subscriptions and gym memberships, and later received forgiveness on each loan. He was indicted last summer on 27 counts.

stories.headline: Last suspect sentenced in connection with Aurora teen's death
stories.summary:
April Collingwood, 46, was sentenced Monday to 22 years in prison for first-degree burglary with assault or menacing, the last sentencing in the shooting death of an Aurora teenager. Court records show eight other charges were dismissed under a plea agreement.

Murder charges against Collingwood and two other men were dismissed by prosecutors in early 2025. The victim, 16-year-old Audrina Arrington, a student at North High School in Denver, was killed Jan. 7, 2025, in an apartment in the 10600 block of East Jewell Avenue in Aurora.

According to an arrest affidavit, two men went to the apartment at the behest of a woman who had been told that three stolen motorcycles and tools could be found there.

stories.headline: Denver police seek information about hit-and-run, Stout Street shooting
stories.summary:
The Denver Police Department asked the public Friday for help solving two open cases. The first is a hit-and-run that seriously injured a bicyclist around 6:25 p.m. Oct. 13 at North Speer Boulevard and West 14th Avenue.

Police say a northbound motorist struck the bicyclist, who was riding eastbound in a marked crosswalk, and fled without providing required information. The suspect vehicle is a blue 2010 Toyota Prius, Colorado plate AANP17, that may have damage to the driver's side front bumper and hood.

The second case is a shooting around 7:42 p.m. Oct. 8 in the 2100 block of Stout Street that injured two people, who are expected to survive. The suspect is described as a Black man wearing a black Champion hoodie, a blue bandana over his face and black and white athletic shoes. Tips can be given to Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-7867.

stories.headline: Denver Waymos are being egged
stories.summary:
Since Waymo's robotaxis began operating in Denver on Sept. 1, riders have reported vandalism in the form of egging. Denver resident Connor McGriff heard two eggs hit the windshield of his Waymo around 6 p.m. Oct. 11 near Lincoln Street, close to Capitol Hill.

McGriff said the vehicle did not appear to detect the impact and the ride continued normally. The friend who ordered the car did not report the incident to Waymo or police. In another case, Jeff Hunley posted a TikTok video of a man in a nearby car throwing eggs at his Waymo on Sept. 24; Waymo refunded him and he did not file a police report, according to KDVR.

Several such incidents have been filmed and posted online in recent weeks. Waymo operates in 15 cities, and Denver is one of several to see vandalism of the vehicles, some of it more extreme, including in California.

stories.headline: Colorado wildfire activity quiet, with prescribed burn near Red Feather Lakes
stories.summary:
Colorado wildfire activity is quiet, with no major active wildfires burning across the state. No Red Flag Warnings or fire weather watches are in effect, and significant fire potential is low statewide through midweek.

Mild daytime conditions and occasional gusty afternoon winds persist along parts of the northern Front Range and eastern plains. Cooler overnight temperatures and recent mountain precipitation are suppressing fire behavior.

U.S. Forest Service crews are conducting the Magic Feather Prescribed Burn near Red Feather Lakes in Larimer County, which is producing visible smoke. Controlled burns may resume on Boulder County open space as weather permits, and fire districts remind residents that slash pile burning requires adequate snow cover.

stories.headline: John Beake, general manager of Broncos' Super Bowl teams, dies at 87
stories.summary:
John Beake, who was instrumental in the trade that brought John Elway to Denver and helped guide the Broncos to back-to-back Super Bowl titles in the late 1990s, has died at age 87, the team said Saturday.

Beake served as general manager of the Broncos' 1997 and 1998 Super Bowl-winning teams. 9News described him as a nice man with a friendly laugh and a loving husband and father.

His role in the Elway trade and the championship era made him a significant figure in franchise history.

stories.headline: Colorado Rapids earn scoreless draw in Portland, hold ninth in Western Conference
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rapids played to a 0-0 draw Saturday night at Providence Park in Portland, keeping them ninth in the Western Conference with 39 points. They trail the LA Galaxy by one point and the Seattle Sounders by three. The eighth- and ninth-place teams meet in a single-elimination match for a playoff berth.

Colorado dominated possession and controlled early play but could not score. Goalkeeper Nico Hansen made two strong saves in the second half and recorded his seventh shutout of the season. It was Colorado's 10th clean sheet, fifth most in MLS.

Coach Matt Wells praised the team's mentality after Wednesday's 2-2 draw with Minnesota United, in which mistakes and a red card hurt the Rapids. Colorado returns home to face the Vancouver Whitecaps.

stories.headline: Michigan sweeps top-ranked DU Pioneers in marquee hockey series at Magness Arena
stories.summary:
No. 2 Michigan swept a two-game series at Magness Arena against top-ranked Denver, which played without star goaltender Johnny Hicks. The Wolverines won 4-1 Friday, after Denver raised its 2026 championship banner, and 4-3 Saturday.

Saturday's game was a physical slugfest featuring two Denver goals waived off after review and a review that awarded Michigan the game-winner. It was Michigan's first trip to Denver since 1981, and the teams met in a double-overtime Frozen Four game in April won by DU.

Coach David Carle said the Pioneers learned much from the weekend and should not get wrapped up in results. Michigan defenseman Landon Dupont, projected as the top pick in the 2027 NHL draft, missed Friday but returned Saturday.

topStory.headline: Oil Prices Slip as U.S. Waiver on Russian Sanctions Raises Supply Hopes, but Gulf Attacks Limit Decline
topStory.summary:
Crude oil prices fell Monday as traders weighed the prospect of more Russian supply reaching global markets after President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday waiving most U.S. sanctions and tariffs on Russia. Brent crude futures fell 2.38% to $107.25 per barrel in one report, while West Texas Intermediate lost 1.78% to $99.60. Other outlets recorded different levels at various points in the session. One showed Brent down 1.5% at $108.22 and WTI down 0.6% at $100.85, and another showed WTI dropping below $97.00. Crude had surged nearly 5% last week, and WTI remains more than 8% higher for the month and nearly 40% above its July lows.

The executive order suspended numerous sanctions on Russia days before they were set to take effect and waived proposed tariffs on countries importing Russian oil. Trump said the waiver was in the national interest and came a week after he signed a diesel import deal with Russia and blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian facilities for driving up global fuel prices. In a weekend social media post, he said he was negotiating a Russia-Ukraine peace deal and did not want to drive Moscow from the bargaining table. Secretary of State Marco Rubio asked for more time Saturday to assess the situation, and Trump told reporters in Florida, "A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out," leaving the administration's final stance unclear.

The waiver drew criticism from European officials and from Republican and Democratic lawmakers in the United States. Ukraine signaled it will continue attacking Russian infrastructure while lamenting additional agreements between Washington and Moscow. Fires broke out at an oil terminal and depot in St. Petersburg after a large Ukrainian drone strike Sunday, according to Governor Alexander Beglov. The terminal exports about 120,000 barrels per day of refined products, mostly fuel oil, per Kpler data, and the extent of damage was unclear. Ukraine had briefly paused strikes on Russian energy facilities after Trump declared Oct. 11 that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to a truce.

Security in the Persian Gulf region has also deteriorated. Two tankers were attacked off the coast of Saudi Arabia on Friday, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre: one was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubayl, and the ST3 was struck by an unknown projectile. The UN's top maritime official said 24 vessels have been attacked in the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said a tanker "violating regulations" caught fire after striking a sea mine. Iran has escalated attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman to choke off regional crude exports. Supertanker freight rates have reached record levels and insurers have raised premiums, which analysts say should cushion prices.

The developments come as rising fuel costs weigh on the Republican Party's prospects in the November midterm elections. Critics have predicted the Russian waivers will do little to lower diesel prices, arguing the price spike stems chiefly from Trump's war against Iran, which has battered Middle Eastern flows. ANZ analysts said the key question is whether the global supply chain can efficiently deliver refined products to end users, noting that oil demand has stayed resilient despite high prices. Upbeat Chinese third-quarter GDP data and a third straight monthly rise in Chinese refinery throughput offered limited support to prices, and markets are watching for clarity on the sanctions decision and developments in the Gulf.
